title: Advanced composites, additive manufacturing, and forest-derived materials

runs.v: Two distinct openings sit in this cluster.

First, qualification and certification workflow for additively manufactured parts entering naval service. PNSY has proven the technical path with the copper-nickel flange, which moves the bottleneck to paperwork, inspection, and weld qualification rather than printing. Software that compresses AM part certification has a named customer in-state and a Navy-wide market behind it.

Second, and less obvious, a defense material qualification path for cellulose nanofibril. Feedstock pilot production, composite fabrication, and accredited ballistic testing all exist inside the University of Maine System, and nobody has assembled them.
Nanocellulose has been ten years away from commercial scale for about fifteen years. Two tons per day is a pilot rate.
Anything here is a materials qualification problem with a long timeline, competing against carbon fiber and UHMWPE incumbents that carry decades of qualification data.

Maine has more space infrastructure, more companies, and a more coherent state strategy than the sector usually gets credit for. The constraint is launch. Everything else here is open.

The Maine Space Corporation is a quasi-state body created by the Legislature in 2022, headquartered in Hangar 5 at Brunswick Landing. Its strategy, set out in Maine Space 2030, is a three-part complex spanning several locations: an innovation hub, a research and development element, and a launch element. Enabling legislation limits launch activity to small satellites and small rockets, and anything larger needs the Legislature to act again.

Executive Director Terry Shehata has been explicit about the ceiling. Maine is not trying to be a Cape Canaveral of the north. The state is pursuing a share of the new space economy on terms that fit its politics, which is the same reason the coastal launch plans stalled.

The SpaceTech Facility in Hangar 5 at Brunswick Landing, opened 24 October 2025 alongside the Maritime Industrial Workforce Training Center. A 1,300 square foot lab and collaboration hub with a thermal chamber and equipment simulating launch, transport, and operational environments. Capabilities cover qualification of electronics and hardware for space, prototyping, advanced materials research, and reliability testing for consumer and industrial products. The state's first space qualification testing facility.

The Maine Space Corporation is looking to place small satellite testing hubs in Aroostook and Washington counties and in western Maine, so companies elsewhere in the state can reach qualification testing without driving to Brunswick. Shehata's stated goal is all elements of the space complex operational within five years.

Brunswick Executive Airport, with 18 aerospace tenants, two 8,000-foot former Navy runways, 650,000 sq ft of hangar and maintenance space, established UAS operating procedures, more than 27,000 annual flight operations, and rocket engine test capability. Subject to the AFFF constraint in section 7.
Loring in Limestone, with two 12,100-foot runways, the longest in Maine, uncongested airspace, and a launch already flown from it.
High-latitude geography suited to polar and sun-synchronous orbit access, plus the Andover earth station heritage.
The Maine Space Grant Consortium, and a 50-plus organization NSF Regional Innovation Engines coalition across Maine and New Hampshire.

Biomanufacturing is where the state is furthest from its own potential. Maine argues it is 4.7 percent defense by share of GDP and holds three life science institutions of national standing with zero defense engagement between them. Feedstock resilience, fermentation capacity, and domestic biomanufacturing are named priorities with a real capacity problem, and Maine has the aquaculture sector, the forest bioproducts base, and a genomics institution to characterize any of it.
None of this requires new institutions. It requires naming the ones that exist.

First, a potential demand node. Medical countermeasure development for chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear agents requires animal-model testing, and BARDA runs a standing Broad Agency Announcement soliciting that work through 2028, with a parallel USAMRDC announcement alongside it. Maine has run a Three-Port Strategy since 1978, splitting cargo development across Portland, Searsport, and Eastport while keeping the rest of the coast for fishing and recreation. The Maine Port Authority is a quasi-state agency under MaineDOT. The state has put close to $100 million into the three ports since 2009.

Deep-draft, ice-free, naturally sheltered, 48-foot draft. Second-largest tonnage seaport in New England and a major petroleum port. The International Marine Terminal is a 33-acre facility at 460 Commercial Street with a container crane, a refrigerated container yard, and a rail connection. TWIC required for cargo delivery.

Eimskip made Portland its primary US port of call in 2013 after evaluating Boston, Rhode Island, and Portsmouth, and runs a weekly Green Line service. Portland to Reykjavik is roughly seven days, extending to the Faroes, the UK, Scandinavia, the Baltics, and the Mediterranean, with Asia connections by transshipment at Reykjavik. Eimskip is also the terminal operator. Volumes reached roughly 50,000 TEU in 2023 and grew about 3 percent in 2025 against tariff headwinds.

A reefer rack expansion toward roughly 420 containers ran over budget at $17.8 million with about $14.3 million federal, and MARAD approved a de-scoped plan. MaineDOT also holds a Clean Ports Program planning grant.

Searsport at Mack Point is the energy port, with preliminary design and permitting work for offshore wind port infrastructure at Mack Point or Sears Island. Eastport is the deepest natural seaport in the continental United States, handles vessels up to 900 feet, and is commercially in a slump. Its recent federal work is a breakwater wingwall extension and fish pier repair.

entries.title: The Arctic Security Cutter homeport question

runs.v: The Coast Guard is building 11 Arctic Security Cutters, contracted across Rauma Marine Constructions in Finland, Bollinger in Houma, and Davie Defense at Helsinki, Galveston, and Port Arthur. First delivery is expected by the end of 2028. The first three go to Alaska, two at Kodiak and one at Seward, which leaves eight homeports undecided.

On 6 July 2026 Sen. Angus King wrote to Commandant Adm. Kevin Lunday urging the Coast Guard to select Maine for at least one. His argument is geography, deep-water access, shipbuilding and repair capacity, and Arctic expertise, naming Portland and Eastport as the candidate ports and citing UMaine Arctic research and Maine Maritime Academy as the sustaining ecosystem. Coast Guard Sector Northern New England is already headquartered in South Portland.
King co-chairs the Senate Arctic Caucus with Sen. Murkowski, chairs the Strategic Forces Subcommittee, and travelled to Greenland in early 2026. This is a serious push rather than a press release.
